extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and comedy writers working on crowd work and live performance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for stand-up comedians on performing crowd work and controlling a room during live sets, distilled from a TV episode review. Focuses on interaction, presence, material angle, and handling difficult responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have A Strong Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian needs a strong opinion — not just observations but an actual, unique perspective. Jokes tend to land differently when it feels like the comedian genuinely believes something about the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without that unique-to-them view, material can feel flat even if joke structure is solid. Aim to convey genuine belief about the subject; make your perspective evident in set-up and punch. (Original phrasing: 'Stand-ups don’t just need observations, they have to have an actual perspective, a unique perspective.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk To, Not At
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work should feel like real, live, in-the-moment, on-the-spot interaction — a conversation with the audience rather than fishing for banal content or talking at people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for natural, relaxed exchanges that include the crowd and lower tension. Avoid forced prompts or obvious setups that make the audience feel like props. Effective crowd work makes people feel included, not singled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work With What You’re Given
rubrics_metrics.description: When crowd responses fall flat or energy shifts unexpectedly, comics should not blame the audience but adapt and use whatever response they get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bad audience responses as part of the process. Instead of fighting or forcing a prepared bit, pivot, riff, or reframe using the actual input. Example note from the page: 'Bad audience responses are part of the process, work with it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay Connected
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain connection to the room by repeating audience members’ names and details and by actively pulling the whole crowd into the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple moves (e.g., asking the room to repeat a greeting) loosen the atmosphere and give interactions shape. Even when addressing one person, keep the whole audience engaged so they feel part of the exchange rather than distant observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charisma Counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage presence and charisma matter: stronger performers command attention before the punchline and can earn audience trust faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charisma can change how material lands and helps the audience start trusting a comedian before they’ve fully earned it via jokes. Work on delivery, timing, and presence as much as on writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to introduce difficult or uncomfortable topics while keeping things light — finding the right wording and pacing is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best comics ease audiences into uncomfortable territory rather than trapping them there. Test phrasing carefully and avoid moving too heavy too quickly. (Referenced idea: a joke is good if you can 'get away with it' — wording matters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Find Your Angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is not just new topics but a distinctive angle on familiar subjects; approach a familiar subject 'sideways' with your particular lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences have heard broad topics before; what they haven't heard is your specific perspective. Make material simultaneously general enough to relate and particular enough to be fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen Closely
rubrics_metrics.description: Good crowd work requires truly receiving what the audience gives and doing something with it, rather than forcing a prepared direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize active listening so you can build on audience cues. Weaker moments arise when comedians force prepped bits instead of staying with real-time responses. Listening enables meaningful, responsive riffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Shock and Humiliation (Anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on shock, humiliation, or mean-spirited tactics to control the room is a lazy and often ineffective approach to crowd work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The episode highlighted that the strongest crowd interactions weren't the harshest ones; they came from comics who stayed present, likable, and kept the audience with them. Use empathy and presence rather than humiliation to gain control.
